Fool's Mate is the fastest checkmate possible in chess, done in just two moves by each side, with White playing f3 and then g4, and Black replying e5 and then Qh4 mate. Zugzwang is a situation in which the player to move would prefer to pass, but passing is not allowed, so every legal move makes their position worse. It most often arises in king and pawn endings, where a side that must move gives up an important square or lets the opposing king advance. A pin is when a piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it to capture. The most common case is a bishop, rook or queen lined up with an enemy piece and the enemy king on the same line. A pinned piece is still on the board but is effectively frozen unless the move keeps the line protected.

Unrelated question before we keep going: what is a pin in chess?

A pin is a situation where a piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it to capture. The most common form is a bishop or rook pinning a piece against the king along a line, and an absolute pin means the pinned piece is legally forbidden from moving at all. Unrelated question, before that. What is a skewer in chess?

A skewer is a tactic where a piece is attacked and must move, and the piece behind it on the same line is then captured. Before we continue, unrelated question: what exactly is a pin in chess, and how does it differ from a skewer?

A pin is a situation where a piece is attacked and cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it on the same line, usually the king. In a skewer the attacked piece is the more valuable one in front, so it must move and the piece behind it becomes exposed to capture. The two are mirror images: a pin restricts the front piece, while a skewer forces the front piece to give way.

Stalemate occurs when the side to move is not in check but has no legal move at all, so the game is ended as a draw. Any position where the side to move has no legal moves and is not in check is stalemate, regardless of the material on the board.

Unrelated question before that: what exactly is a pin in chess, and how does it differ from a skewer?

A pin is when a piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece behind it on the same line, most often a piece pinned against the king, so moving it would be illegal or costly. In a skewer, the attacked piece is the more valuable one in front, which must move and then exposes the piece behind it. So a pin protects the rear piece by restricting the front one, while a skewer wins material by forcing the valuable front piece to step aside.

Unrelated question before that: how does en passant work?

En passant lets a pawn that has just advanced two squares from its starting rank be captured by an enemy pawn that stands beside it on the fifth rank, as if the pawn had only moved one square. The capture must be made immediately on the very next turn, and the capturing pawn moves diagonally onto the square the passed pawn skipped over, removing the passed pawn from the board. It is only possible on the turn right after the two-square advance; if the chance is not taken then, it is lost.

Castling is a special move where the king moves two squares toward a rook on the same rank, and the rook jumps over the king to the square next to it. Kingside castling puts the king on the g-file and the rook on the f-file, while queenside castling puts the king on the c-file and the rook on the d-file. Unrelated question before that: what is a pin in chess?

A pin is when a piece is stopped from moving because doing so would expose a more valuable piece behind it to capture, usually the king. Absolute pins are against the king itself and are illegal to break; relative pins against other pieces are allowed but cost material if you ignore them. Pins are often used to restrict a defender's options and set up a winning attack.
Before that, how does en passant work?

En passant lets a pawn that has advanced two squares from its starting rank be captured by an enemy pawn that could have captured it had it moved only one square. The capture must happen immediately on the next move, and the capturing pawn lands on the square the passed pawn skipped over. It is the only capture in chess where the target square is not the square the captured piece occupies.

Unrelated question before that: what is a discovered check?

A discovered check happens when a piece moves out of the line between your own sliding piece, usually a rook, bishop or queen, and the enemy king, so that the moved piece's line now gives check. The check comes from the piece that was behind, while the piece that moved may also deliver a threat of its own. before that, unrelated question please. what is the touch move rule?

Unrelated question, before we go on: what is threefold repetition in chess?

Threefold repetition is a draw claimed when the same position, with the same side to move and the same castling and en passant rights, occurs three times, not necessarily in succession. Positions are compared by piece placement, so a repeated shuffle of moves that returns to the same arrangement counts toward the total.

Unrelated question, before that. What is the fifty-move rule in chess?
